16.content: who belong to the world of

fills.notes: The sentence needs an appositive identifying the Smoke-king as the primordial leader emerging from the depth; in the substrate he functions as the first instigator of conflict and so is introduced as the first ruler among the dark worlds.

fills.fill: according to her image, hard and
fills.notes: The clause explains the bodily property (hard/tough) by reference to Matter as the forming matrix; the substrate speaks of formation ‘according to the image/nature’ of Matter, yielding hardness and cruelty.
After ‘nor any iron implement, can … him and cut him’, the required verb is ‘cleave/sunder’.
Completes the intensifier before ‘strong and hard’, matching the parallel earlier ‘very tough’.
Thunder-like speech is then compared to the sound produced by stones; ‘crashing’ fits the acoustical correspondence (violent collision = outbreak of strife).
Completes the comparison: thunder resembles the crashing of rocks when they break; this supports the war/rupture correspondence.
Pairs naturally with ‘cries out’, marking escalating vocal terror; the substrate emphasizes sound as a power of domination.
‘calls … over his powers’ needs an adverb of proclamation/command.
Bird-simile requires a passive fear-response before a stronger bird; matches ‘tremble and totter and fall’.

fills.fill: at the hawk / or the eagle
fills.notes: The comparison is to smaller birds falling when confronted by a raptor; hawk/eagle aligns with the dark-world bestial correspondences and the earlier eagle-mark among the shapes.

fills.fill: who is the chief of them all,
fills.notes: The phrase must bridge ‘King of all the mountains of Darkness’ to an identifying epithet; the substrate typically uses a rank-formula (‘chief of them all’) rather than devotional titles.
The close of the description wants a temporal seal tying his birth to the primordial uprising of Darkness; ‘from the beginning’ matches ¶2–3 framing.

fills.fill: who belong to the world of

assessment: Most gaps are small and could be restored by tight syntactic constraints (articles/letters, required verbs). The hardest place is ¶9 (multiple sound/bird similes), where the correspondential direction is clear (terror-sound like thunder/rocks; lesser powers like birds before a raptor) but exact zoological wording is not uniquely constrained; those restorations remain tentative.
